name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Republican voters declare their freedom from the Freedom Caucus
description: As someone who is lucky enough to offer commentary about South Dakota politics, I must note that the recent Republican primary has made my job tougher. The state’s Republican voters, without any regard for my feelings, kicked out most of the members of the South Dakota Freedom Caucus. Don’t get me wrong, I was usually […]
text:
Voters fill out their ballots at a Sioux Falls polling place during the South Dakota primary election on June 2, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)As someone who is lucky enough to offer commentary about South Dakota politics, I must note that the recent Republican primary has made my job tougher. The state’s Republican voters, without any regard for my feelings, kicked out most of the members of the South Dakota Freedom Caucus.
Don’t get me wrong, I was usually on the other side of any issue that they proposed. But I was a fan. Never famous for their legislative successes, caucus members were as feisty as they were misguided.
Caucus shenanigans were usually good for two or three columns every legislative session. While other legislators were busy passing bills and debating the budget, Freedom Caucus members, all of them Republicans and most of them in the House, could be counted on for making headlines for all the wrong reasons.
Republican voters once again opt to oust incumbents from South Dakota Legislature

Remember Rep. Logan Manhart of “white boy summer” fame? With only a few ill-chosen words on Instagram he used his freedom of speech to not only raise his political profile but simultaneously anger the state’s nine Native American tribes.
The group’s lone senator, John Carley, was noted for pushing a bill that would have made the Ten Commandments required reading in South Dakota classrooms. His legislation also mandated that the Ten Commandments be posted in schools.
Ever the joker, Carley played an intense game of “Hide the State Senator” during a critical vote on economic development incentives for data centers. Emerging from seclusion the next day, he said that his absence was due to an eye doctor appointment.
Personal freedom meant so much to Rep. Dylan Jordan that he was willing to risk millions of dollars in South Dakota’s federal funding just because he felt too constrained by the state’s seat belt law. Now there’s a freedom fighter.
Rep. Josephine Garcia rose to be chairwoman of the Medical Marijuana Oversight Committee. Undaunted by voters’ 70% approval of medical marijuana in 2020, she loaded a committee hearing with anti-marijuana speakers and then claimed she was just doing her job. She’s a guerrilla fighter for freedom.
Rep. Heather Baxter came in third in a three-way race for two House seats in her district. That won’t matter to her since she has already announced her intention to challenge Secretary of State Monae Johnson at the Republican convention. It turns out that Johnson was not enough of an election denier to suit Baxter. She said she’s aligning herself with President Trump, who is famous for believing that if an election’s outcome doesn’t suit him, it must be rigged.
The Freedom Caucus website notes that not all Freedom Caucus members are public members. It seems that for some people, their love of freedom must be a private matter. Here’s hoping for my sake that some of the extra-secret members of the caucus got reelected.


Let us know what you think...


 

The one member of the Freedom Caucus who escaped the wrath of voters was their leader, Rep. Phil Jensen. Jensen has a resume of legislative run-ins that’s as battle-scarred as it is long. He was stripped of the vice chairmanship of the House Education Committee because of his legislation that sought to deny the Huron School District its state funding because he had heard bad things about the district’s bathroom policy.
He got kicked off that committee and reassigned to another when a committee seating arrangement impinged on his freedom. When he disparaged the religious beliefs of his colleagues, he was kicked out of the Republican caucus for two weeks. Maybe that gave him more time to meet with the secret members of the Freedom Caucus.
It’s hard to say why so many members of the Freedom Caucus were shown the door in the latest primary. Maybe South Dakota voters just don’t like freedom. Or maybe they’ve grown tired of a group that values political gamesmanship over legislative success.
Whatever the reason, voters have shown a callous disregard for me and what I’m going be able to write about during the next legislative session.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Fifty for 150: Pope John Paul II in 1993 at center of Colorado’s biggest gathering
description: “In the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, I say to you, good morning!” Those were the first words spoken by the headliner at the reputed largest gathering in Colorado history, which took place on the morning of Aug. 15, 1993, at Cherry Creek State Park southeast of Denver.  The speaker […]
text:
Pope John Paul II visits Denver during World Youth Day in August 1993. Young people give John Paul a Mile High welcome as he greeted them from his popemobile at Mile High Stadium on Aug, 12, 1993. (Glenn Asakawa/Donated to the Denver Public Library by the Rocky Mountain News )“In the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, I say to you, good morning!”



This story is part of Colorado at 150.


Those were the first words spoken by the headliner at the reputed largest gathering in Colorado history, which took place on the morning of Aug. 15, 1993, at Cherry Creek State Park southeast of Denver. 
The speaker was Pope John Paul II, and the gathered were 375,000 people who were part of the culminating event of World Youth Day, a periodic Roman Catholic Church production that promotes faith among young believers. The pope led a three-hour mass at the park for a throng that included participants from 70 different countries.
World Youth Day was actually a multi-day affair, and the pope had arrived several days earlier. His presence in and around Denver brought the attention of the world to Colorado, and it dominated activities throughout the metro area. President Bill Clinton and Vice President Al Gore were in town for the event. So were “19 cardinals, 450 bishops, 3,000-plus media representatives” and 186,000 youth attendees, according to The Rocky Mountain News. A National Park Service incident report records that at one point the pope took an hour-long hike in Rocky Mountain National Park, which prompted a multi-agency security operation that included the Secret Service. 


In a measure of the scale of the event, McDonald’s set up 70 tents with grills and propane burners at the site of the mass. It was the largest operation in the restaurant’s history.
World Youth Day was not without its conflicts. The pope, whose anti-abortion stance was his main message at the event, drew objections to the church’s anti-LGBTQ+ positions, and gay and lesbian Catholics rallied at the state Capitol in anticipation of the pope’s visit. 
“We challenge the pope to seek hope and peace and justice for all people, especially the graceful, the beautiful and the queer people of God,” said Kevin Calegari, president of DIGNITY/USA, an organization of gay and lesbian Catholics.
The mass itself was marred by mass illness. Many of the “pilgrims” who attended walked 15 miles from Denver to the park in temperatures approaching 100 degrees Fahrenheit. They “dropped like flies,” according to one account, and paramedics raced around in golf carts trying to treat them all. The Arapahoe County sheriff deployed a tractor-trailer full of an intravenous solution for dehydration patients. A 61-year-old man died of a heart attack.
But others noted a perceived positive influence of World Youth Day, which occurred during the so-called Summer of Violence in Denver, when the media played up fears of youth involved in gang activity.
In a day-after report on World Youth Day, The Rocky Mountain News wrote, “Mostly, Denver seemed graced by a remarkable period of tranquility. The summer of violence subsided, and the city was charmed by another face of youth. Confrontational abortion protests were called off. Even the Rockies baseball team had its longest winning streak.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska’s once-controversial ‘500-mile Sculpture Garden’ celebrates 50 years
description: To mark America's 250th birthday, the Nebraska Arts Council is planning a series of events to celebrate the sculptures installed for the bicentennial in 1976.
text:
"Erma's Desire," an abstract sculpture by Johnny Raimondi, was not only the largest in Nebraska's I-80 Bicentennial Sculpture Garden, but the most controversial. Some saw sexual innuendo in its design; others wondered whether sculptures of covered wagons or cowboys would be more appropriate. (Photo by Jeannine Conry)LINCOLN — A collection of outdoor sculptures that stirred criticism and conversations 50 years ago is about to take another ride into the spotlight.
To mark the 250th birthday of the United States, the Nebraska Arts Council is planning a series of events to celebrate the eight sculptures placed at Interstate 80 rest stops as part of the nation’s bicentennial in 1976.
The largest and most controversial of the sculptures, entitled “Erma’s Desire,” sparked nationwide publicity after some Nebraskans saw sexual innuendo in its spike-like towers, and questioned what contemporary art has to do with the state’s heritage.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“What’s the matter with cowboys on horses or covered wagons?” David Breslow, a member of the Nebraska Highway Commission told a UPI reporter in 1975. “These are the kinds of things that ought to be on our rest stops.”
 

A series of events will celebrate the 50th anniversary of Nebraska’s 500-mile Sculpture Garden:

June 30, 5:30 p.m., Sheldon Museum of Art, Lincoln. A panel discussion featuring sculptor Johnny Raimondi, Art Thompson, head of state bicentennial commission, and art historian Karen Janovy.
July 1, noon, Museum of Nebraska Art, Kearney. Raimondi discusses his sculpture, “Erma’s Desire,” the I-80 project and his other sculptures in the state.
July 1, 3:30 p.m., Grand Island east rest stop, site of Erma’s Desire. Celebration of the sculpture.
July 1, 6 p.m., Stuhr Museum, Grand Island. Talk by Raimondi and reception.
July 2, 6 p.m., Joslyn Museum, Omaha. Raimondi talk and reception.
July 3, 10 a.m., York westbound rest area. Celebration of “Crossing the Plains,” by sculptor Bradford Graves.
July 3, 4:30-6 p.m., Museum of American Speed, Lincoln. Reception for Raimondi. (RSVP requested)
July 4, 10 a.m., Civic Center, Seward. Raimondi talk.
July 4, 1 p.m., Blue River eastbound rest area, near Seward. Commemoration of “Arrival” by Paul von Ringelheim, along with program featuring State Poet Jewell Rodgers and judi gaiashkibos, executive director of the Nebraska Commission on Indian Affairs.



For a time, the Hall County Board denied a building permit for Erma’s Desire. And the State Legislature debated whether to accept the sculptures. The project was delayed six months by the kerfuffle.
But Erma and her companions persisted, and the artist who created Erma’s Desire, Johnny Raimondi, still marvels at the publicity generated by a piece intended to honor his mother’s wishes that her sons find fulfilling lives and careers.
“The title, they thought it had to do with sex. But I’m so happy about that. It was in every newspaper in the United States,” Raimondi said in a telephone interview from his home in Florida.
 Art to honor the state’s heritage
The “I-80 Nebraska Bicentennial Sculpture Project” was conceived by the Nebraska American Bicentennial Commission as the state’s way to honor the founding of the nation in 1776.
Back then, there had been talk of erecting a massive football player to span the Interstate (with a restaurant in its helmet) as a way to attract tourists and honor the Nebraska football team’s successes.
But Norman Geske, then the director of the Sheldon Museum in Lincoln, had been appointed to help the commission to commemorate the bicentennial. He considered the football player, and another proposal to erect a mastodon along I-80 to be “ludicrous,” according to Karen Janovy, who had worked with Geske at the Sheldon.
“We’ve got to put a stop to that,” she quoted Geske as saying. The two leaders of the state bicentennial commission, Art Thompson and Tom Yates, agreed.
Geske knew all the important sculptors in the U.S., Janovy said, after establishing a sculpture garden at the Sheldon in 1970. So he reached out to them to submit proposals.
The project evolved to place 10 outdoor sculptures at I-80 rest stops, from Ashland to Sidney, that would reflect the state’s heritage. It became known as “Nebraska’s 500-mile Sculpture Garden.”
Janovy, who will participate in a June 30 panel discussion about the history of the sculptures, said that Geske felt the project’s top purpose was educational. He wanted to look into the future, she said, and not backwards to the pioneer days.
 Local residents warmed to the project
Local communities were involved, and local buy-in was sought, said Markey. Once local residents got to know the sculptors, they warmed to the project, he said.
“In 1976, the idea of contemporary sculpture was kind of unknown to Nebraska,” Markey said. “It really awakened people to what public art can do for a community.”
“That’s one of the things we’re trying to highlight this year (see sidebar).”
Back in the 1970s, each state was provided $100,000 from a national bicentennial commission to celebrate the event. That, Markey said, provided seed money to attract private donations for the project, which cost upwards of $800,000.  No state tax dollars were used.
Raimondi, who now has three other outdoor sculptures in Nebraska, said that his original concept was for a massive Erma that spanned across the Interstate. But that proved too expensive, as did commissioning 10 sculptures.
 Sculptures maintained with set aside funds
Of the original eight works, seven survive and they are carefully maintained by the Arts Council via funds set aside for that purpose.
Nebraska’s windy weather claimed the 35-foot-tall, brushed aluminum tubes of “Roadway Confluence,” also known as “Bionic Bunny,” by Hans Van de Bovenkamp. So that sculpture, near Sidney, was removed in 2011, Markey said, after several attempts to salvage the piece failed.
Another piece, “Nebraska Wind” by George Baker, originally floated in a pond at the westbound rest stop near Kearney.  But the piece kept breaking away from its moorings, so eventually, it was placed on dry land, Markey said.
“We just had everything maintained and conserved over the summer,” he said. “There was very little work that had to be done.”
Florida-based sculptor Johnny Raimondi will headline several events in June and July to commemorate the 50th anniversary of Nebraska’s unique “500 mile sculpture garden” at Interstate 80 rest stops across the state. (Photo by Ralph Cantin)
Raimondi, who was the youngest sculptor chosen at age 28, said he was thrilled to get the commission. He, like the other sculptors, lived in Nebraska as they created their works. A metal fabricator in Grand Island helped create and install Erma’s Desire, he said.
The sculptor, who will talk at a series of events in late June in Nebraska, now has three other sculptures in the state, including the soaring “Dance of the Cranes” at the entrance of Omaha’s Eppley Airfield.
Markey, of the Arts Council, said that the I-80 sculptures came before placing modern, conceptual artwork in public spaces was widespread. And before communities learned how a work of art – think “The Bean” in Chicago – could become a must-see landmark.
Now, he said, there are several sculpture gardens across the state. Directions and information about them will be placed at the I-80 sculpture sites, along with new interpretive signs providing more information about the works and the artists.
This year’s commemoration includes several programs at I-80 communities, including at the Museum of Nebraska Art at Kearney, the Stuhr Museum in Grand Island, the Joslyn Museum in Omaha and the Sheldon in Lincoln.
The idea is to inspire discussions about art, and the sculptures placed along Nebraska’s interstate 50 years ago, Markey said.
“Public art is a reflection of the people in the communities both then and now, and in the years to come,” he said. “We all learn from public art and what it says to us.”
Nebraska’s “500-mile Sculpture Garden” was conceived as a way to commemorate the bicentennial of the United States in 1976. Fifty years later another celebration of the public art project is planned in 2026. (Courtesy Nebraska Arts Council)

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: OPINION: Rising childcare costs strain Nebraska family budgets, reduce business output
description: For many Nebraska families, childcare is not affordable. A new calculator created by First Five Nebraska illustrates those costs.
text:
Child care that is high quality and affordable is vital to Nebraska's economy. (Stock photo by Lourdes Balduque/Getty Images)One of the most common questions First Five Nebraska (FFN) receives from policymakers and community leaders is “What’s the average cost of childcare in Nebraska?” The short answer: more than most families in our state can afford. The actual answer: it’s complicated.
The price that a family pays for child care isn’t straightforward – it depends on the number and age of their children, their preferences and needs, the type of child care available in their community and how all these factors contend within their family’s current financial situation.
That’s why FFN created the Nebraska Child Care Affordability Calculator. This interactive tool shows how licensed child care costs fit, or more often, do not fit, within the budgets of Nebraska families with young children. It accounts for the factors that affect what families pay for child care, along with other major household expenses. Here’s how it works:

Choose the location you want. Select the Nebraska county, and the calculator will automatically calculate the median income for families with children in that county.
Want to look more closely at income? The calculator will allow you to select different income levels. The calculator will automatically compute 185% of the federal poverty level ($59,477 for a family of 4), which is the economic reality for 1 out of every 3 children in Nebraska under age 6. You can also choose the federal poverty level ($32,150 for a family of 4) or enter a custom amount.
Change the family size or the number of children in child care by adjusting the household composition. How will a new baby change a family’s child care expenses?
The calculator automatically selects family child care as the default setting—in Nebraska, 2 out of every 3 licensed child care providers are family child care homes, which are typically the more affordable option. The majority of licensed child care slots, however, are in center-based programs. Changing this selection will automatically calculate the price of care based on the most current Nebraska Market Rate Survey. You can also manually change the prices based on your knowledge of the local market.
The calculator also automatically computes typical large expenses for families. You can customize housing expenses (rent/mortgage, utilities), transportation (car payment and gas), health insurance, and food costs.
Finally, the calculator includes an “Other” category for additional expenses families may need to include in their budgets. Although it is automatically set to “0,” we challenge you to think about which expenses aren’t included—clothing for growing children, diapers, toiletries, surprise repairs, savings, student loans, and more.

The Nebraska Child Care Affordability Calculator makes visible the financial pressures that Nebraska families with young children face every day. Child care costs are rising faster than inflation, placing increasing strain on middle-income families. At the same time, child care programs throughout the state are struggling to bring in enough revenue to cover the costs of providing quality care. Child care businesses are engaging in a difficult balancing act—raising tuition is necessary to keep their programs open, but this risks pricing families out of the market.
And it’s costing Nebraska. Inadequate access to child care leads to an estimated $1.74 billion in lost business output and $1.61 billion in lost labor income annually.
Our hope is that the calculator will actively inform policy conversations that directly affect the financial well-being of households with young children in care. If our state wishes to live up to its promise as a desirable place to live, work and raise a family, it is crucial to have a clear view of the child care-related financial pressures facing families and how policy decisions impact those we are counting on to sustain our communities, grow our economy and raise the next generation of Nebraskans.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: New rules for 4-day school weeks draw pushback from some rural North Dakota schools
description: The North Dakota Department of Public Instruction is weighing new rules for four-day-a-week K-12 schools, but some educators say the proposed changes would unfairly burden rural schools. Under the four-day-a-week model, districts still must still meet the same requirements for minimum instruction time, so school days are longer. Districts that want to adopt[...]
text:
Shannon Faller, high school principal for Alexander Public Schools in northwest North Dakota, testifies at a hearing on new proposed rules for four-day school weeks on June 4, 2026 at the North Dakota Capitol. (Photo by Mary Steurer/North Dakota Monitor)The North Dakota Department of Public Instruction is weighing new rules for four-day-a-week K-12 schools, but some educators say the proposed changes would unfairly burden rural schools.
Under the four-day-a-week model, districts still must still meet the same requirements for minimum instruction time, so school days are longer. Districts that want to adopt the schedule must apply for approval from the Department of Public Instruction.
According to the state agency, 15 school districts have made the switch so far. An additional four were recently approved to move to a four-day-a-week schedule for the 2026-2027 school year. All of the districts serve rural areas, including several tribal communities.
Many educators and leaders from districts who have gone to a four-day system say it has helped improve the quality of their instruction, student attendance and teacher retention and recruitment.
Alexander Public Schools, a district in northwest North Dakota, has used the four-day school week model for the past eight years. 
“This started as a student-driven initiative in our district,” Alexander High School Principal Shannon Faller said at a recent public hearing on the potential amendments to four-day-a-week regulations. “They saw it through with the administration and our community.”
New rules
The Department of Public Instruction is considering adopting new rules that would change the criteria it uses to determine if school districts qualify for the four-day-a-week system.
The agency under the current rules must determine whether the change is likely to produce any of five possible benefits: Encouraging innovation in teaching, improving academic outcomes and opportunities, allowing greater flexibility in how school facilities are used or producing significant cost savings for the district.
The proposed amendments would eliminate cost savings and facility use from the list, focusing only on academic factors instead. 
Superintendent of Public Instruction Levi Bachmeier said the agency’s objective is to make the criteria “only about what’s happening in the classroom.” 
Some educators and administrators who testified at the hearing pushed back on the idea of only evaluating the model based on how it affects learning. 
Schools — especially those with small class sizes — can see large fluctuations in test scores from year-to-year based on the makeup of their student bodies, they said.
“One challenging year should not place an entire district’s calendar structure at risk,” Faller said.
Several school district representatives during the hearing also said while the rules ask schools to display “innovation in teaching” and to improve “educational outcomes,” it doesn’t adequately define those terms.
Under the current rules, once a school is approved for the four-day week schedule, it must apply to renew its permission the following year. If a second year of four-day school weeks is approved, the school can request to continue the system for an additional one or five years. The proposed amendments wouldn’t change this.
Whether schools receive reauthorization for the schedule depends on how well they meet evaluation criteria. Bachmeier said the Department of Public Instruction’s priority is ensuring four-day schedules don’t negatively impact students’ ability to learn.
Multiple educators and administrators during the hearing said they don’t think the success of the four-day system can be fairly evaluated in such a short time frame.
Rep. LaurieBeth Hager, D-Fargo, who sits on the House Education Committee, said during the hearing she thinks the proposed changes are too significant to be adopted through rulemaking.
“I’m confused that this is an administrative rules hearing,” she said. “I’m looking at amendments to law.”
Hager said that the changes should be brought during the upcoming legislative session, where there would be more opportunity for public comment and the proposed amendments would have to be vetted by lawmakers.
Leslie Bieber, superintendent of Alexander Public Schools, said in an interview the four-day schedule is overwhelmingly popular with the district.
She said teachers value the ability to spend an extra day a week with their families, and feel that the longer school days allow them to plan lessons more effectively. A survey found that 95% of parents, 96% of students and 97% of staff support the four-day weeks, Bieber said.
McClusky-Goodrich Schools, a district in central North Dakota, was recently approved to switch to four days a week. Superintendent D’Aulan Bussman said she’s hopeful the alternative setup will help the district attract and retain teachers.
Some staff have told her they are searching for other jobs but will stay if the four- day model is adopted, Bussman said. 
She added that her district will be actively monitoring test scores and is open to reverting to the five- day weeks if they prove to be a better fit.

title: Five laws passed by Tennessee lawmakers in 2026 face legal challenges, so far
description: Tennessee officials were sued again this week, marking five laws passed by the state legislature in 2026 facing legal challenges. The latest lawsuit filed by the Financial Technology Association challenges the legality of a new law that would impose a $10 fee and 2% tax on international money transfers. The law was passed as part […]
text:
Tennessee continues to get lawsuits challenging legislative action with five new laws facing legal action. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee officials were sued again this week, marking five laws passed by the state legislature in 2026 facing legal challenges.
The latest lawsuit filed by the Financial Technology Association challenges the legality of a new law that would impose a $10 fee and 2% tax on international money transfers.
The law was passed as part of state Republicans’ Immigration 2026” agenda, coordinated by House Speaker Cameron Sexton and White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller. The international money transfer tax is designed to make it more expensive for immigrants to send money back home, which they often do to support families they left behind when coming to the United States for work.
The Financial Technology Association, in its filing in Davidson County Chancery Court, argued the new law discriminates against a specific transaction, violating the Commerce Clause of the U.S. Constitution. The association is made up of two dozen companies, like Amazon, PayPal, SoFi and Stripe.
Tennessee officials have faced an increasing number of lawsuits over the years as lawmakers have become more comfortable challenging federal laws and targeting localities. Lawmakers have also increased the state Attorney General Office’s budget to fight these suits.
In 2023, lawmakers were sued half a dozen times by the Metro Nashville government over bills that would have given the state greater control over the city. Most have been unsuccessful, including one to take control of the Nashville Airport Board with a majority of state appointees.
Republican lawmakers decided in 2026 to pass legislation taking over all the airport boards in Tennessee, not just Nashville’s, hoping it would lead to a better outcome in court. The Metro Nashville Airport board sued the state in federal court over the law this week.
CVS sues Tennessee over pharmacy benefit manager monopoly law

Other lawsuits this year included multiple challenges to the state’s new U.S. House map and CVS and Cigna’s challengese to a law banning certain Pharmacy Benefit Managers.
The international money transfer law challenge is the second lawsuit filed against one of the new immigration laws passed this year.
The ACLU and National Immigration Law Center filed a legal challenge earlier this month to a new Tennessee law that makes it a crime for immigrants without legal status to enter or remain in the state.
The federal lawsuit argues that it violates the Supremacy Clause of the Constitution because Tennessee is trying ot enforce immigration laws reserved for the federal government.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota Republican ‘populists’ earn the boot
description: Many candidates of the misnamed “populist” faction of the North Dakota Republican Party were shown the door in the June 9 primary, as voters who voted on the GOP side of the ballot gave most of them the boot. Ironically (or is it stupidly?), a focused clique has cleverly seized control of the party by […]
text:
Voters fill out and turn in ballots during early voting at the Bismarck Event Center on June 8, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)Many candidates of the misnamed “populist” faction of the North Dakota Republican Party were shown the door in the June 9 primary, as voters who voted on the GOP side of the ballot gave most of them the boot. Ironically (or is it stupidly?), a focused clique has cleverly seized control of the party by stuffing local meetings with their wrong-headed fans, and by intimidating long-time traditional Republican conservatives who showed up at those meetings, and were not welcome. It’s a pattern that has been repeated for several years, and the result has been a complete takeover of the leadership, a circumstance which, as primary election results confirm, has made the party’s endorsements irrelevant.
The primary vote revealed there is nothing “populist” about the splinter group running the NDGOP. Populist implies the people are with the politicians and that politicians represent the people. The results June 9 showed that Republican voters don’t view the splinter group that way at all. In district after district from east to west, north to south, many incumbents and newcomers who embraced the faux populist moniker were sent packing. Among them were six of the Legislature’s reliable culture warriors, the lawmakers whose priorities gum up the process while they pursue issues that belong in families, churches and a doctor’s office, not in legislative committee rooms. 
 
More election 2026 coverage


Gov. Kelly Armstrong, who has been censured twice by the clueless leadership of his party, had a good day June 9. Of the 18 Republican legislative candidates he endorsed, 17 won. Most of the losing candidates identified with the party’s bumptious leaders. Emboldened by his success, the governor said the NDGOP-endorsed candidates ought to call for a change in party leadership.
If legislative results were not enough to confirm the party leadership’s irrelevance, the results for statewide offices should. All the Republicans who were challenged in statewide balloting won by landslide margins over the party’s endorsed candidates. For example, Congresswoman Julie Fedorchak faced for a second time the party-endorsed Alex Balazs, besting him with 73% of the vote to his anemic 27%. Two years ago in a four-way tilt, she beat him with 46% to his 4%. Given that lopsided loss and across-the-board losses in other statewide races, and the near wipeout in legislative races (and a few local elections), it’s reasonable to wonder whether the party’s leaders are slow learners.
Gov. Armstrong has read the political tea leaves correctly. He has not hesitated to criticize the supercilious cabal that has taken over his party. He understands that the vast majority of Republican voters are not obsessed with going-nowhere divisive culture wrangles. They want elected leaders to focus on maintaining the good governance that has distinguished 30 years of traditional conservative legislating in North Dakota.
The primary balloting on the Republican side should convince sensible legislative leaders to quit accommodating the culture warriors. While several were ousted in the primary, others remain in the Legislature, and no doubt will attempt to advance an agenda of book banning, curriculum interference, theocratic rule and violations of personal privacy. Most North Dakotans, including most Republicans, want none of it. The primary showed as much.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Schools, nonprofits try to keep WV kids fed this summer amid grocery price hikes, welfare changes
description: The West Virginia Department of Education is working with local partners this summer to provide statewide feeding sites for those 18 years old and younger, working to put together  nutritious meals while navigating surging food costs.
text:
A child eats a free breakfast through the county’s summer feeding program at Elk Center Elementary in Charleston, West Virginia, on June 16, 2026. (Photo by Marcus Constantino for West Virginia Watch)The air in the school gym smelled like homemade biscuits.
Kanawha County Schools cook Marsha Burns spent the morning at Elk Center Elementary in Charleston, West Virginia, making biscuits with a new white wheat flour produced in West Virginia. She added a crispy sausage patty from a local meat supplier.
Later, dozens of children rushed into the kitchen to fill up their trays with breakfast food through a free summer program provided through the county school system. 
“A lot of times this is the only time these kids will eat,” Burns said on June 10. 
West Virginia has one of the nation’s highest child hunger rates, and one in five children face not having enough to eat. Most counties offer free breakfast and lunch to all students during the school year.
This summer, there are added strains on families to keep food on the table without the help of school year meal programs. Grocery prices rose 2.9% in April compared to the same month last year, according to government figures released in May. Fruits and vegetables have seen some of the biggest price hikes.
The West Virginia Department of Education is working with local partners this summer to provide statewide feeding sites for those 18 years old and younger, working to put together nutritious meals while navigating surging food costs. It is made possible through U.S. Department of Agriculture funding.
“It really has been skyrocketing pretty bad, but we try to give the kids what they don’t even get at home,” said Lori Lanier, a specialist for child nutrition with Kanawha County Schools.
In a news release, State Schools Superintendent Michele Blatt said meals will be readily available this summer across West Virginia. “This reassurance is important now more than ever,” she said.
Kanawha County Schools Cook Marsha Burns hands a child a biscuit during free breakfast at Elk Center Elementary in Charleston, West Virginia, on June 10, 2025. (Photo by Marcus Constantino for West Virginia Watch)
Food assistance program changes likely to impact children
President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act is also likely to impact child hunger in West Virginia after it included changes to food assistance for 36,000 low-income West Virginia residents. The state’s Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program enrollment declined by 5.7% between enactment and February 2026 since the megabill was implemented.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, West Virginia children were automatically enrolled in a Summer EBT program that provides money for groceries. Now, automatic eligibility is tied to enrollment in federal anti-poverty programs or Medicaid. Everyone else must submit an application. 



Quotation







If you can't see feeding hungry children as a priority, it seems to say a lot about you.


– Senate Minority Leader Mike Woelfel, D-Cabell


“Summer EBT has been a critical tool for helping put food on families’ tables during the summer when school meals are not available. The cuts Congress made to SNAP last summer via the One Big Beautiful Bill mean that the Summer EBT program will reach fewer children in West Virginia this year,” said Kelly Allen, executive director at the West Virginia Center on Budget and Policy.
Across the state, summer feeding programs are preparing for increased need.
In Preston County, 700 children have signed up to receive free meals this summer. The county’s summer feeding program will offer grab-and-go food boxes, providing 10 breakfasts and 10 lunches each time. 
Preston County Schools Nutrition Director Justin Hough
“We’ve seen an increase in need,” said Justin Hough, director of nutrition for Preston County Schools. He said that even if families receive state food assistance, the current inflation rate “doesn’t mean they’re able to make up for all those lost meals that they would rely on during the school year.”
The Lincoln County Family Support Center Big Ugly Community Center in Harts expects to serve dozens of students for eight weeks this summer with hot meals on site. The center sends students home with a backpack of non-perishable foods to feed them over the weekends. 
“It’s very critical. It’s their source, because they don’t have it,” said Candy Vannatter, site director at the Big Ugly Community Center. The center’s food pantry is serving an increased number, too.
Senate Minority Leader Mike Woelfel, D-Cabell, tried for years to establish a “Summer Feeding for All” program. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Senate Minority Leader Mike Woelfel, who is concerned about children accessing food in summer, has tried for years to convince the Legislature to establish a “Summer Feeding for All” program.
The measure didn’t mandate that counties establish summer feeding programs, but Woelfel wanted counties to work on identifying the number of children who are hungry to help local resources meet the demand.
The bill passed the Senate in 2023, 2024 and 2025 but wasn’t taken up by the House of Delegates. This year, Woelfel’s legislation got held up in the Senate Finance Committee under Republican leadership. The bill had a zero cost but was referred to that committee before it could come to the floor for a vote. 
“I’m just disappointed,” said Woelfel, D-Cabell. “We spent more time in the Senate trying to pass legislation to compel the state police to sell hundreds of machine guns to West Virginians than we did on this bill.”
Woelfel is retiring this year after more than a decade in the Senate. He is hopeful other Senators will champion the bill next year. 
“There’s so many people in the Legislature that always want to use the word, and I’ll put it in quotations, ‘Christian,’ but I know a couple of senators that have told me privately the government has no responsibility to take care of somebody’s kids, so that’s the great one of the great ironies of that place,” Woelfel said. “If you can’t see feeding hungry children as a priority, it seems to say a lot about you.”
Elk Center Elementary in Charleston, West Virginia, will serve free breakfast and lunch to children up to 18 years old this summer. (Photos by Marcus Constantino for West Virginia Watch)
Preparing children’s meals amid soaring grocery prices
Hough said the federal reimbursement rates for summer feeding groceries “aren’t quite keeping up with the rate of inflation.”
“We were at least very fortunate that our contract with our food distributor can only be increased to a certain amount throughout the course of the contract, so that has allowed us to offset some of our costs a little bit,” he said, adding a $9,000 grant from No Kid Hungry is helping offset costs. “But definitely we’re having to get a lot more creative in our meals and our meal patterns to try not to go over budget.”
Kanawha County Schools Executive Director of Child Nutrition Diane Miller said their budget costs are up 15%. (Photo by Marcus Constantino for West Virginia Watch)
Diane Miller, executive director of child nutrition for Kanawha County Schools, said their budget is up 15% for regular food costs as they operate 15 feeding sites for children up to 18 years old.
“We really have to refocus if we’re going to spend our money wisely,” she said. “We’re focusing on the quality items that I can find, but most importantly, I’m trying to find that we can use less paper along the way, or find an alternative.” 
Miller plans to use many locally-produced meats and vegetables, like potatoes and green beans; the cooks have been helpful in learning new recipes with local products, she said. 
“We only succeed when the students attend, and they are having a ball, and they’re actually helping me to pick what they want to see in the meals,” Miller said.  “These programs are here now to help you stretch your dollar a little bit farther.”

text:
States Newsroom graphic illustration New Developments


An Israel-based wave energy company is in talks with Florida Atlantic University and University of Michigan in an effort to advance its operational intelligence system, WaveGPT. In addition to filing a Testing and Expertise for Marine Energy Application alongside Florida Atlantic University, Eco Wave Power is exploring a potential joint grant application, intended to create a wave-powered coastal data center.

A Kalamazoo marijuana company is offering up its processing facility for data center development, according to a report from MLive’s Aya Miller. Harbor Farmz announced in a June 9 press release that it was engaging with engaging with interested developers, infrastructure investors, commercial real estate professionals, site selectors and technology-sector stakeholders in hopes of redeveloping the facility into a data center amid a saturated cannabis market. CEO Michael Ward told MLive that if they were to sell the building, they would continue to do business in another location.

Updates


On June 8, dozens of Lyon Township residents packed into a planning meeting to voice their opposition to a proposed six-building data center, after the developer’s legal team sent a letter demanding the township’s planning committee take action. The project, which would be developed by Verrus and Walbridge, would encompass 1.8 million square feet along Grand River Avenue, WXYZ’s Jeffrey Lindblom and Faraz Javed report. Among those speaking in opposition was state Senator and Michigan Republican Party Chair Jim Runestad (R-White Lake).

Hundreds of residents filled a barn in Lowell Township as the planning commission heard a proposal from Microsoft to develop a five-building data center campus. MLive’s Ehren Wynder noted the company had not sought a recommendation to approve its site plan and zoning ordinance amendment request at the June 8 meeting, but hundreds of residents in attendance made it clear they did not approve of the project.
The Vevay Township Board of Trustees unanimously voted against entering negotiations with the City of Mason for a land transfer agreement for the purpose of developing a data center, Todd Heywood reports for WLNS. The proposal would have allowed the two municipalities to share tax revenue on the land.
Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel has filed testimony with Michigan energy regulators asking for additional safeguards for residential customers as DTE Energy and and Google seek approval on a contract to supply power to a 1-gigawatt data center. In her testimony, the attorney general argued the current protections are inadequate, and that the Michigan Public Service Commission must do more to ensure residents do not see additional the costs as a result of the data center.

News of Note

Rachel Crowther, a Democrat from Rockford running to represent Michigan’s 90th state House District released a statement on June 8, backing three protections for data centers setting up shop in West Michigan. She called for independent environmental study requirements, full disclosure of any chemicals used in cooling and industrial processes, and meaningful engagement with residents. She also voiced support for legislation creating a one-year moratorium on data center development. Crowther is unopposed in the primary, while Lynn Afendoulis, Susannah Watts, Andrew Jackson Willis and Jordan Youngquist are slated to face off in the Republican primary.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: The hidden costs of going month-to-month on your lease in Idaho are growing
description: What would you do if your rental costs doubled next month? In Idaho, some landlords and management companies impose steep month-to-month lease fees that can do just that. A month-to-month fee is an additional charge added to monthly rent in exchange for the flexibility of a short-term lease agreement. Often, these fees take effect once […]
text:
(Photo by Getty Images)What would you do if your rental costs doubled next month? In Idaho, some landlords and management companies impose steep month-to-month lease fees that can do just that.
Idaho US Sen. Crapo’s 2025 housing survey identifies housing challenges faced by Idahoans

A month-to-month fee is an additional charge added to monthly rent in exchange for the flexibility of a short-term lease agreement. Often, these fees take effect once a standard 12-month lease ends if the tenant does not sign a new long-term lease.
In a rental market that has become increasingly unaffordable for many Idahoans due to stagnating wages and the state’s recent housing boom, these fees may become the breaking point for some of Idaho’s most vulnerable renters, leading to housing insecurity and even homelessness.
 Idaho renters already under pressure

According to the National Low Income Housing Coalition, nearly 50% of Idaho’s low-income renters are cost-burdened, spending more than 30% of their monthly income on housing. Those struggling with high rents include working families, seniors on fixed incomes, and people living with disabilities.
In Boise, a worker must earn roughly $35 an hour to afford the average two-bedroom apartment. For someone earning minimum wage, that would require working 154 hours per week to afford the same apartment.
 When a lease renewal costs hundreds

For Idaho tenants, the realities of month-to-month leasing can be devastating. These fees often range from $200 to $500 per month, with some renters reporting charges nearly equal to their monthly rent. For many already struggling to keep up with rising housing costs, these additional fees are simply unaffordable.
Many Idaho leases automatically convert to month-to-month agreements after the initial lease term ends. Under Idaho law, landlords may increase rent with just 15 days’ notice before the lease expires. At the same time, landlords have full discretion in setting lease fees and rental increases.
Landlords do face legitimate concerns when tenants are not locked into long-term leases.
Turnover costs, uncertainty and administrative work are real considerations for landlords and property managers. However, charging hundreds of dollars each month goes far beyond covering administrative costs and instead becomes one more expense many Idaho tenants simply can’t afford.
 The repercussions of month-to-month fees on Idaho tenants

At Jesse Tree, a nonprofit focused on homelessness prevention through eviction intervention, staff have seen an increase in tenants citing month-to-month fees as a major source of financial hardship. One tenant living on a fixed income had consistently paid rent on time before a hospitalization prevented them from signing a new 12-month lease. Because their lease automatically converted to month-to-month, they were charged an additional $500 monthly fee they could not cover, and subsequently ended up in eviction court on account of it.
There are many reasons why someone may not immediately sign a new lease agreement: health emergencies, hospitalization, work schedules, transportation barriers, family crises or simple miscommunication. Yet for many Idaho renters, failing to complete that additional administrative step can trigger hundreds of dollars in added housing costs almost overnight.
 Idaho can do better

Idaho is a place where many people still believe hard work should be enough to stay housed. However, when renters who are already struggling face hundreds of dollars in additional fees because of a missed appointment, a hospitalization or a delayed lease renewal, we must question whether our housing system is serving our communities fairly.
Month-to-month lease fees may be legal, but that does not always make them reasonable. At a time when so many Idaho families are already one emergency away from losing their housing, costly fees on top of already unaffordable rents pushes more people toward housing instability.

title: WV voters support keeping school vaccine mandates, poll finds
description: Most voters in West Virginia support keeping school vaccination requirements, according to a poll released last week.  The poll found that 69% of the state’s electorate and 57% of the state’s likely Republican primary voters are opposed to eliminating school vaccine mandates.  The poll was conducted in February 2026 by Virginia-based political polling agency[...]
text:
A poll was conducted by Virginia-based political polling agency Cygnal and the Infectious Disease Prevention Network found that 69% of the state’s electorate and 57% of the state’s likely Republican primary voters are opposed to eliminating school vaccine mandates. (Getty Images)Most voters in West Virginia support keeping school vaccination requirements, according to a poll released last week. 
The poll found that 69% of the state’s electorate and 57% of the state’s likely Republican primary voters are opposed to eliminating school vaccine mandates. 
The poll was conducted in February 2026 by Virginia-based political polling agency Cygnal and the Infectious Disease Prevention Network, a pro-vaccine advocacy organization. It included 500 from the electorate broadly and 388 likely Republican primary voters. 
Besides West Virginia, the agency polled 12 other Republican-leaning states: South Carolina, Idaho, Montana, Texas, Florida, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa, Louisiana, Oklahoma, Kansas and Arkansas. 
A majority of the overall electorate in each of the states and a majority of GOP voters in six of the states oppose eliminating school vaccine requirements, the poll found. 
“I think there’s a perception that Republicans in particular, are very divided on this issue, and what we found in West Virginia, and frankly, across 13 other Republican states as well is that there’s a very clear two-to-one opposition to eliminate vaccine mandates over and over and over again,” Chris Lane, senior partner and pollster for Cygnal, told West Virginia Watch. “It kind of just tends to be the louder voices on both sides that I think create the perception, but the numbers are extremely clear.”
All states require that school children be vaccinated against a series of infectious diseases including polio, measles and chickenpox. Florida announced it aims to end all vaccine mandates, including those for school students. 
The poll specifically asked if voters support or oppose West Virginia adopting a policy similar to Florida’s.
The majority of the poll was conducted by online surveys sent via text message. Poll participants are selected by a number of factors including history and whether they said they were likely to vote in the Republican primary this year, Lane said. 
“There’s a bunch of validators that we use to make sure that the people we’re talking to actually represent what a Republican primary voter audience is supposed to look like in West Virginia,” Lane said. “And then we have a bunch of quotas that we insist on hitting that are perfectly representative by gender, by age, by education level, by different parts of the state, by ideology, by race, by income, and by voter history.”
The general electorate poll had a margin of error of 4.38% and the Republican voter poll’s margin of error was 4.97%. 
Lane said margin of error is less important in a poll than effective sample size, which he said his firm uses. 
Erin Abramsohn, executive director of the Infectious Disease Prevention Network, said the organization did the survey to better understand what voters think about vaccines and public health policy. 
“Our polling helps states understand that vaccine access and confidence are often much more nuanced than the public debate suggests,” she wrote in an email to West Virginia Watch. “Most people still want access to vaccines, trust their healthcare providers, and support policies that keep communities healthy.
“We use polling data to help shape legislative strategy, inform communications, support local advocates, and help elected officials feel confident supporting policies that preserve access to vaccines,” she said. 
She added that the polling helps the organization measure public support for vaccine access and protections, identify effective messages, and give policymakers credible data they can use when making decisions. 
This is not the only poll that has indicated West Virginia residents’ support for school vaccine requirements. A September 2025 West Virginia MetroNews poll found that 71% of respondents support keeping school vaccine requirements. A July 2024 poll by the West Virginia Chamber of Commerce found that nearly 80% of 600 respondents think healthy students should get vaccinations against childhood diseases. 
Poll didn’t address exemptions
The Infectious Disease Prevention Network poll did not include questions about whether West Virginia voters support adding religious and philosophical exemptions to the state’s school vaccine requirements, an issue the state Supreme Court is expected to rule on.
West Virginia is among five states with laws that do not allow families to opt out of the school vaccine requirements because of philosophical or religious objections to the shots. 
Gov. Patrick Morrisey issued an executive order requiring the state health department to allow religious exemptions soon after he took office in January 2025. The order is based on the state’s 2023 Equal Protection for Religion Act. 
Morrisey did not rescind his order after lawmakers in 2025 rejected a bill that would have codified religious exemptions. 
Raleigh County Circuit Judge Michael Froble ruled in November in favor of families who are suing the state and Raleigh County boards of education over their refusal to allow students to attend with a religious exemption. 
The boards have appealed the decision to the state Supreme Court.  
A spokesman for Morrisey did not respond to a request for comment about the poll.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee’s “Nuclear Family Month” is a slap in the face of dads fighting for their children
description: A few weeks before the climactic conclusion of the 114th General Assembly, a resolution by Rep. Bud Hulsey, a Kingsport Republican, was signed by Gov. Bill Lee, declaring the month of June as Nuclear Family Month. Rather than focus time and energy on infrastructure and affordability, Hulsey prioritized a fatuous resolution aimed at thwarting the […]
text:
Rep. Bud Hulsey, a Kingsport Republican retiring in 2026, sponsored a resolution to name June "Nuclear Family Month." (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)A few weeks before the climactic conclusion of the 114th General Assembly, a resolution by Rep. Bud Hulsey, a Kingsport Republican, was signed by Gov. Bill Lee, declaring the month of June as Nuclear Family Month.
Rather than focus time and energy on infrastructure and affordability, Hulsey prioritized a fatuous resolution aimed at thwarting the perceived attacks on the nuclear family model in Tennessee.
Hulsey may as well have been Don Quixote riding through a field of windmills — a man with an inflated sense of self swinging at empty air.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Hulsey wasn’t the only faux warrior waving the nuclear family sword, however. Seventy-two other representatives voted in favor of a resolution that included several reductionist gems, such as:
“Children without fathers are ten times more likely to abuse chemical substances.”
“Fatherless youths are twenty times more likely to be incarcerated.”
“71% of high school dropouts are from fatherless homes.”
When Lee signed the resolution officially making June “Nuclear Family Month,” I immediately became defensive of my LGBTQ+ friends who celebrate Pride Month each June. I assumed this was just another irresponsible swipe at a group of Tennesseans who were simply living their lives.
After reading the resolution, however, I finally had an inkling of what it felt like to be needlessly attacked.
I’ve been a full-time single father for the last five years. My daughter moved to Tennessee to live with me after her 8th-grade year. Being a parent to her, by myself, is singularly the most joyful experience I’ve ever had.
For most of her childhood, my daughter lived with her mother just outside of Dallas. Every other Friday, I would leave my house around 2 a.m. to make sure I made it to her elementary school to volunteer in the lunchroom — opening Lunchables, GoGURTS, and Capri-Suns.
On those Friday afternoons, I would stand outside of the school, waiting with the other parents, extending my 6-foot-2 frame so my daughter could see me above everyone else. Our weekend would begin.
For nearly a decade, I built some semblance of a sporadic life every other weekend in the suburbs of Dallas. I drove through tornadoes, ice storms, and, worst of all, the state of Arkansas to make sure I was being the parent I needed to be.
As June kicks off Pride celebrations, Tennessee designates it ‘nuclear family month’

Nuclear family be damned.
In 2016, I found myself in Chancery Court simply trying to increase the number of phone calls with my daughter from twice a week to five. After a day of testimony and cross-examinations, a judge inexplicably took parenting time away from me for a reason he chose not to disclose.
Thankfully, his ruling was overturned by the state appellate court several months later. Still, his capricious decision shone a light on a deeper issue in Tennessee — an issue that is only undergirded by misguided resolutions like this one.
If you are a father in Tennessee who is not part of a nuclear family, chances are you don’t see your child nearly as much as you would want. Because custody time is often based on the vague idea of the best interests of the child, judges in Tennessee often default to a standard 80/20 rule for custody time. 
In studies published by Custody X Change, an independent software firm that provides custody scheduling tools for families, Tennessee ranks dead last in the nation for the amount of parenting time awarded to fathers. Fathers in Tennessee average about 22% of parenting time with their child, compared to the national average of 35%.
If there’s any group under attack in Tennessee, it sure as hell isn’t nuclear families.
And if Hulsey and his defenders of prescriptive families truly cared about those bloated statistics in the resolution, they would start asking the right questions rather than drafting ignorant proclamations based on myopic life experiences.
On Sunday, I’ll celebrate Father’s Day with my daughter just as I have every year she’s been alive. She’ll gift me another Jason Isbell T-shirt or a vinyl of my choosing. We’ll talk about what she needs for her apartment in Chattanooga when she begins her sophomore year of college in a couple of months. We’ll take a picture together as we always have, and I probably won’t give a second thought to this toothless resolution.
So, to all the single fathers out there, to all the same-sex fathers who have children, and to all the fathers who are still part of a nuclear family: Happy Father’s Day.
No thin-skinned piece of legislation  can change the important role you play in your child’s life.
